intro: Foundations of International Law. Unit five: general principles of law, unilateral acts, and subsidiary means.

slides.3: The International Law Commission's work on general principles. The Commission took the topic up in 2019 with Special Rapporteur Marcelo Vázquez-Bermúdez. The second report, of 2021, set out the structure now generally used: general principles come in two kinds. Those derived from national legal systems, which require a principle common to the principal legal systems of the world, plus its transposition to the international legal system. And those formed within the international legal system itself. That two-track division is the thing to carry away.
slides.4: What general principles are, and what they are for. Unlike treaties and custom, general principles are unwritten law not created by the will of states — which is why they sit uneasily in a consent-based system. How they are found is contested: by the comparative approach, comparing the principal legal systems; or, some say, by a natural-law approach. The phrase 'civilized nations' in Article 38, paragraph 1, subparagraph c is today regarded as an embarrassing relic, and is read as 'the principal legal systems of the world'. Their purpose is gap filling: they keep a court from having to declare a non liquet when neither treaty nor custom answers the question.
slides.14: Which principles, concretely. J.M.W. versus the European Patent Office names them: the general principles enshrined in the Convention, particularly non-discrimination and the protection of property rights, are part of human rights, which under the tribunal's case law apply to relations with staff. The message is that an international organization cannot treat its staff outside the law merely because its own rules are silent.
slides.15: Unilateral acts: the definition. Acts and declarations made with the intention to create, modify or end international legal rights and obligations. Intention, with an exclamation mark — because that is the whole test. The same words spoken without that intention are politics, not law. Unilateral acts split in two: the fully unilateral, such as recognition and protest; and the partly unilateral, which operate in connection with a treaty — ratification, a reservation, a protest against a reservation.
slides.22: How much weight a subsidiary means carries. Draft Conclusion 3 of the Commission's 2023 work gives six criteria, and they are the answer to the exam question 'how much does this authority prove?'. The degree of representativeness. The quality of the reasoning. The expertise of those involved. The level of agreement among them. The reception by states and other entities. And, where applicable, the mandate conferred on the body. A unanimous Commission conclusion, adopted with a General Assembly mandate and well received by states, sits at the top; a single scholar's article sits far below.
slides.24: What stare decisis means — the definition from Black's Law Dictionary. The policy of courts to stand by precedent and not disturb a settled point: once a court has laid down a principle applicable to a certain state of facts, it will adhere to it and apply it to all future cases where the facts are substantially the same, regardless of whether the parties and the property are the same. This is the common-law doctrine that international law does not have. It is set out here so that you can say precisely what is being denied.
